newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Patten blasts plan to dilute HK civil liberty laws.
newsitem.headline: Patten blasts plan to dilute HK civil liberty laws.

text.p: Governor Chris Patten on Monday attacked Chinese plans to dilute Hong Kong's human rights laws which he said struck at the heart of civil liberties in the territory.
China on Sunday drafted a list of 25 laws, which includes Hong Kong's Bill of Rights and key electoral laws, to be axed or diluted when it resumes sovereignty of Hong Kong on June 30.
Patten in a statement called the proposals misguided and damaging to confidence both at home and abroad.
"They strike at the heart of Hong Kong's civil liberties," he said.
"They appear to be based on politically motivated pretexts rather than real inconsistencies with the BL (Basic Law)."
The Basic Law is Hong Kong's post-handover constitution promulgated by China in 1990.
"Some of them appear to be aimed solely at undermining the legal basis for civil liberties in Hong Kong, and they will certainly have that effect," he said.
"And they are a recipe for confusion and uncertainty in the operation of our legal system after June 30."
Patten accused Chinese officials and Beijing's inner circle of Hong Kong advisers of attempting to ring-fence Hong Kong's post-1997 administration ahead of the handover.

China's Xinhua news agency said the laws were "formulated by the British Hong Kong authorities in an attempt to apply its constitutional bill in violation of the Sino-British Joint Declaration on Hong Kong", the 1984 treaty on the handover.
It said Britain had introduced "principles which contravene the Basic Law and agreements reached by the two governments".
Britain had repeatedly urged Beijing to reject all proposals to gut the Bill of Rights and to reinstate obsolete legislation.
